title: A Giant X-Ray Flash May Have Revealed a Brand-New Magnetar
summary:
Imagine two stars the size of cities crashing together far out in space. That crash can send out a flash of light so bright we can see it from Earth — even though it happened more than 6 billion years ago, before our Sun was born!

On July 4, 2025, satellites spotted a quick burst of gamma rays (a kind of invisible light) that lasted only half a second. But then something surprising happened: a satellite called Einstein Probe kept seeing bright X-rays from the same spot for nearly 10 minutes. That's the longest-lasting X-ray flash ever seen from a crash like this.

Scientists think the crash was between two neutron stars — the super-dense leftovers of giant stars. When they smash together, they can form a magnetar: a tiny star with a magnetic field so strong it could mess with your phone from thousands of miles away. (Okay, maybe not exactly, but it's really, really strong.)

A scientist named Niccolò Passaleva was on a train when he got the alert. He quickly used a giant telescope in Chile to study the flash. "I was rushing against time," he said.

The flash came from more than 6 billion light-years away. That means the light traveled for over 6 billion years to reach us. Studying it helps scientists understand how stars are born and die — and what weird objects are hiding in space.
why_it_matters: It shows that a flash from an explosion older than our Sun can still teach us something new — and that scientists sometimes make big discoveries while rushing against the clock.

background_read: Neutron stars are the crushed leftover cores of huge stars that blew up long ago. They are only about as wide as a city, yet a single spoonful would weigh billions of tons.
The Einstein Probe is a space telescope launched by China with European partners to hunt for sudden bursts of X-rays and other invisible light from space.
Chile is a long, thin country in South America, and its dry, dark mountains hold some of the world's biggest telescopes because they give super-clear views of the night sky.
Article_Structure: WHO: Satellites such as the Einstein Probe, plus scientist Niccolò Passaleva and other astronomers studying the flash.
WHAT: A half-second burst of gamma rays was followed by nearly 10 minutes of bright X-rays — the longest-lasting X-ray flash ever seen from this kind of crash — hinting a magnetar may have formed.
WHERE: The crash happened more than 6 billion light-years from Earth, and Passaleva studied it with a giant telescope in Chile.
WHY: The light traveled over 6 billion years to reach us, and studying it helps scientists understand how stars are born and die and what strange objects hide in space.

perspectives.description: This is the longest X-ray flash ever recorded from a star smash-up, so it could be our first clear look at a brand-new magnetar being born.
One flash is not proof — astronomers will want more examples before they can be sure a magnetar really formed.
It's amazing that light from a crash that happened before the Sun existed arrived just in time for us to catch it.
